segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you too, who will introduce destructive opinions, even denying the Master who bought them, and bringing swift destruction on themselves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And many will follow them in their debauchery, and because of them the way of truth will be slandered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In their greed they will make money out of you with fabricated words. The verdict against them from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but sent them down to Tartarus in chains of gloom and handed them over to be kept for judgment;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if he did not spare the ancient world, but protected Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood on a world of ungodly people;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if he reduced the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes and condemned them to ruin, making them an example of what is coming for the ungodly;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if he rescued righteous Lot, who was worn down by the debauched conduct of unprincipled people—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormenting his righteous soul over the lawless deeds he saw and heard—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trial and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: especially those who go after the flesh in defiling desire and despise authority. Reckless and arrogant, they do not tremble as they slander the glorious ones,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: whereas angels, though greater in strength and power, do not bring a slanderous judgment against them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But these people, like unreasoning animals, creatures of instinct born to be caught and destroyed, slander what they do not understand, and in the destruction of those creatures they too will be destroyed,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: suffering wrong as the wages of wrongdoing. They count it a pleasure to revel in the daytime. Stains and blemishes, they revel in their deceptions while they feast with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They have eyes full of adultery that never rest from sin; they lure unstable souls; they have hearts trained in greed—children of a curse!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Leaving the straight way, they have gone astray and followed the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the wages of wrongdoing

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but was rebuked for his own lawbreaking: a voiceless donkey, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These people are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm; for them the gloom of darkness has been kept.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For, speaking inflated, empty words, they lure with the desires of the flesh, with debauchery, people who are only just escaping from those who live in error.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They promise them freedom, though they themselves are slaves of corruption; for people are enslaved to whatever has defeated them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if, after escaping the defilements of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and defeated, their last state has become worse than the first.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it would have been better for them not to have come to know the way of righteousness than, having come to know it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed on to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What the true proverb says has happened to them:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “A dog returns to its own vomit,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and, “A sow, once washed, goes back to wallowing in the mud.”

notes.note: The Greek word meant a chosen position, school of thought or faction, and had not yet acquired the later technical sense of “heresy” as officially condemned doctrine. Most versions keep “heresies”; some, like this one, use “opinions,” and “factions” is also possible. The phrase is literally “opinions of destruction,” echoing the “destruction” these teachers bring on themselves.

In first-century Greek this verb covered abusive or defamatory speech against anyone or anything, not only against God. Modern English “blaspheme” is limited to irreverence toward God, so “slander” is used here and in verses 10–12 where the target is the Christian way or angelic beings. Several modern versions keep “blaspheme” or use “malign” or “revile” in these verses.

The Greek verb, found only here in the New Testament, means to consign to Tartarus, the name in Greek tradition for the deep place where rebellious divine beings were imprisoned; Jewish writers in Greek had already borrowed it. It is a different word from those usually rendered “hell” or “Hades,” so the name is kept. Some manuscripts read “pits of gloom” in place of “chains of gloom”; the two Greek words differ only slightly.

The Greek word chiefly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that tests faithfulness, and here it refers to the kind of hardship Noah and Lot lived through. Older versions have “temptations”; most modern versions likewise have “trial” or “trials” here.

The Greek participle is present tense and most naturally means the unrighteous are already being punished while held for the day of judgment, like the angels of verse 4. It can also be read as pointing forward: “to keep the unrighteous for the day of judgment, to be punished then.” Translations and commentators are divided.

The Greek is literally “glories.” Most interpreters take it as a term for angelic beings, as in the parallel at Jude 8, though it is disputed whether good or fallen angels are meant; a minority think of human authorities. “Them” in verse 11 most likely refers to these beings, though some refer it to the false teachers.

Many manuscripts add “before the Lord” after these words, and some read “from the Lord.” The Greek text followed here has neither, and the evidence is closely balanced; many English versions include “before the Lord.”

notes.phrase: in the destruction of those creatures
notes.traditional: shall utterly perish in their own corruption
notes.note: The Greek says “in their destruction they too will be destroyed,” repeating one word-family three times in the verse. “Their” may refer to the animals (these people will die as animals die) or to the false teachers themselves, in which case the noun could mean their own moral corruption. The same Greek noun is rendered “corruption” in verse 19.

notes.phrase: suffering wrong as the wages of wrongdoing
notes.note: The Greek plays on two related words: they are “wronged” as the pay for “wrongdoing,” meaning they are paid back in kind. “Wages” keeps the word’s ordinary sense of a worker’s pay and matches verse 15, where Balaam loves the same “wages.” Some manuscripts read “receiving” in place of “suffering wrong,” which is the reading behind the older English versions.

Some manuscripts read “love feasts” (the community’s shared meals) in place of “deceptions”; the two Greek words differ by two letters, and the parallel at Jude 12 has “love feasts.” The reading “deceptions” is usually judged original here, perhaps as a deliberate play on the other word.

In the Old Testament Balaam’s father is named Beor (Numbers 22:5), and some manuscripts and many English versions have that name here. The best-attested reading is “Bosor,” a form not found elsewhere; its origin is uncertain, and it may reflect a variant pronunciation or a play on the Hebrew word for “flesh.”

notes.phrase: “A dog returns to its own vomit,”
notes.note: The first saying is a loose form of Proverbs 26:11. The second is not from Scripture; it is often compared with a saying in the ancient Story of Ahiqar, and it appears to have been a common proverb. Dogs and pigs were both regarded as unclean animals, which sharpens the insult.

candidates.reason: Used in Acts for a sect or party, in Paul for factions, and here for teachings; the traditional “heresy” is anachronistic, and the split between senses needs fixing once.
Used of God and of Christ (Luke 2:29; Acts 4:24; Jude 4; Rev 6:10) and of slave owners; it should be kept distinct from κύριος “Lord” consistently, with a capitalization rule.
Recurs in vice lists across the Gospels, Paul, 1–2 Peter and Jude, and versions vary among sensuality, licentiousness, debauchery and lewdness.
Spans physical perishing and moral decay in Romans, 1 Corinthians, Galatians and 2 Peter; the sense boundaries and the distinction from ἀπώλεια need one decision.
Frequent term for final ruin (Matthew, Paul, Hebrews, 2 Peter, Revelation) rendered variously as destruction, perdition, ruin or waste; it should be uniform and distinct from φθορά and ὄλεθρος.

findings.problem: παρεισάγω means to bring in secretly or stealthily. Plain "introduce" loses the sense of covert infiltration.
